newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says "mistakes were made" in fundraising.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says "mistakes were made" in fundraising.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday "mistakes were made" in raising money for his re-election campaign, but insisted contributors did not buy influence with him and the system was not corrupt.

At a wide-ranging news conference in the White House East Room that spanned issues ranging from Boris Yeltsin's health to domestic budget concerns, Clinton said an overhaul of U.S. campaign financing laws was long overdue and promised to do all he could to fix the system.

"Nobody is blameless here. It costs so much money to pay for these campaigns that mistakes were made by people who either did it deliberately or inadvertently," said Clinton, who has been under fire since last year's presidential campaign for condoning fund-raising tactics that some critics contend verged on being corrupt.

"It's up to others to decide whether those mistakes were made deliberately or inadvertently," the Democratic president said, alluding to congressional and Justice Department probes. "It's up to me do do what I can to clean up the system."

The president later attended a fundraiser that raised nearly $1 million for the Democratic Party from members of a fund-raising arm, the Democratic Business Council. About 70 people paid a minimum of $10,000 each.

In his opening remarks to the group, Clinton defended his presence at the event as necessary to help the party raise money and insisted he had never made any policy decision based on how it would help financial contributors.
"I never had anyone in four years who asked me to make a decision as president based on being a financial contributor, and I have never made such a decision," he said.

Clinton, who is backing a pending campaign reform measure sponsored by Senators John McCain, an Arizona Republican, and Russell Feingold, a Wisconsin Democrat, admitted at the news conference that it was inappropriate to have a top federal banking regulator attend a May 1996 White House meeting over coffee with more than a dozen leading bankers and Democratic Party fundraisers.

Some of the bankers pumped more than $300,000 into Clinton campaign coffers after the meeting, and the regulator -- Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig -- has said he would not have gone if he had known the nature of the event.

Clinton, who took office for another four-year term eight days ago, said those who donate money to him or his party get only a "respectful hearing" for their money. "Nobody buys a guaranteed result, nor should they ever," he said.

And he defended political fund-raising generally, saying: "I don't think there is anything wrong with raising money for the political process. The problem is the volume of money, the amount of money, the time it takes to raise, the inevitable questions that are raised."

"There is no pattern and practice here of trying to push our systmen over the brink into corruption," he said. "What happens is, there is a race to get as much money as you can to keep from being buried by the other people ... and at the edges, errors are made."
"And when they are made they need to be confessed and we need to assume responsibility for them, and that's what I'm trying to do up here today," Clinton said.

The financing of Clinton's re-election campaign has been a centre of controversy since late last year when it was revealed that Democrats had solicited large sums from Asian business interests with a stake in U.S. trade policy.

The party has voluntarily returned funds that were deemed improperly raised from non-citizens and has also taken several steps to tighten its fund-raising practices, including an outright prohibition on accepting funds from foreigners.
Clinton said laws governing political financing had been passed more than 20 years ago and were now obsolete. "We need to change the system -- it's just outdated," he said.

The campaign financing furore threatens to imperil Senate confirmation of two of Clinton's second-term Cabinet nominees -- Labour Secretary-designate Alexis Herman and Transportation Secretary-designate Rodney Slater.
